hero.t1:
Run a Minecraft server
on your own machine.
hero.sub: ObserverLauncher handles the Java version, the download, the config files, the firewall rule and the backups. You run the server and share the address. No accounts, no telemetry, no subscription — just a launcher that works on Windows and Linux.
demo.t: Everything the launcher tracks, on one screen.
demo.sub: TPS, MSPT, CPU and RAM are sampled once a second from the Java process. Commands run through RCON. Player lists come from the server's own query — the launcher never stores them. Click the sidebar — this mockup is interactive.
ft.sub: Every capability ships with the launcher. No separate tools, no config-file archaeology. Hover or tap a row to expand.
ft.f1d: Vanilla, Paper, Purpur, Fabric, Forge, NeoForge, Folia, Spigot or Velocity — pulled from the official manifest APIs with live version lists.
ft.f2d: TPS, MSPT, CPU and RAM sampled once a second. The UI shows what each number means for your players.
ft.f3d: Modrinth, Hangar and Spigot in one search. Compatibility checks, version picker and per-file download progress.
ft.f4d: YAML, JSON, TOML and .properties with syntax highlighting, validation and conflict detection.
lm.t: What the launcher does not do.
lm.sub: A few things worth saying out loud so expectations match reality.
lm.l1d: This is a desktop launcher, not a hosting service. When your PC sleeps, the server stops. You provide the hardware and the network.
lm.l2d: The launcher opens the Windows Firewall for you, but your home router's port-forwarding rules are yours to set. The UI shows the exact address to share.
lm.l3d: Your server files stay on your disk. There is no account, no telemetry and no sync between machines. That is by design.
lm.l4d: Only Java Edition servers are supported. Geyser/Floodgate work as regular plugins if you want Bedrock players to join.
cm.t: Where it wins, where it doesn't.
cm.sub: Pick the right tool: a local launcher is not a cloud host, and that's fine.

faq.sub: Anything else — open an issue on GitHub.
faq.a1: Yes — MIT licensed, forever. No ads, no accounts, no telemetry, no premium tiers.
faq.a2: It's fully open source — every line is auditable. Servers are downloaded only from official APIs (Mojang, PaperMC, Fabric, Forge…) and the launcher never sends your data anywhere.
faq.a3: Depends on your Minecraft version. The launcher checks this automatically and can install the right Java with one click, no admin rights required.
faq.a4: All of them that your chosen software supports — version lists are loaded live from official APIs, from 1.8 to the newest release.
faq.q5: Can my friends join from anywhere?
faq.a5: Friends on your WiFi connect directly. For friends elsewhere you'll need to forward a port on your router — the launcher shows the exact address and can open Windows Firewall for you.
faq.a6: Yes — browse modpacks right in the marketplace and import a full pack in one click. The launcher downloads every mod and config file for you; no manual zipping, no missing dependencies.
faq.q7: How much RAM do I need?
faq.a7: The launcher itself idles around ~150 MB. The server is the hungry part: 2–4 GB is a sane start for a small Paper or Vanilla world; modpacks want more. You set the memory slider yourself.
faq.q8: Does it need internet all the time?
faq.a8: Only for downloads — server jar, Java, plugins. Once everything is local, a LAN world runs with the cable unplugged.
faq.q9: Can I run it on a VPS or headless?
faq.a9: It's a desktop app with a GUI. On a VPS you'd just run the jar directly; a CLI mode is on the roadmap.
foot.dis: ObserverLauncher is an unofficial tool, not affiliated with Mojang or Microsoft. Running a server requires accepting the Minecraft EULA.
